sections.b: The angel of the LORD promises a son to Manoah's barren wife and makes him "God's Nazirite from the womb": no razor is to touch his head, and he will "begin to rescue Israel" from the Philistines (Judges 13:5). The mother keeps the Nazirite food rules while she carries him. The chapter's hero is arguably the mother, who sees and understands more than her husband. Samson's name comes from shemesh, "sun."

sections.h: A strongman led by his eyes (Judges 14–15)
sections.b: Samson wants a Philistine wife because "She is right in my eyes" (Judges 14:3), and the narrator says the LORD was using it to strike at the Philistines (Judges 14:4). The Spirit sweeps down on him to kill a lion, thirty men of Ashkelon, and a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone. Yet his fights are personal revenge, his own tribe of Judah hands him over (Judges 15:11–13), and his first prayer is a complaint of thirst (Judges 15:18).

sections.h: Delilah and the death in Gaza (Judges 16)
sections.b: After three false answers, Samson tells Delilah his secret; she shaves off his seven braids, and "the LORD had left him" (Judges 16:20). Blinded and grinding grain in prison, he is brought out to amuse the crowd at Dagon's feast. He prays, "Lord GOD, remember me, please!" (Judges 16:28), and pulls down the building, killing more in his death than in his life.

Hebrews 11:32–34 counts him among those who were made strong out of weakness. Augustine defended his death as commanded by the Spirit (City of God 1.21). The rabbis honored him as a judge but taught that he followed his eyes and lost them (Mishnah Sotah 1:8). Modern readers range from seeing a tragic hero (Milton) to a self-centered vigilante, to a picture of Israel itself: set apart, drawn to foreign partners, captured and blinded, yet heard when it calls on God (Greenstein, Webb).

common: Samson's strength was in his hair, but the text says it came from the Spirit of the LORD and left when the LORD turned away (Judges 16:20).
Delilah was a Philistine; the text does not say so.
uncommon: Some scholars read Samson as a figure for the nation of Israel, chosen from birth yet unable to resist foreign gods and partners.
In the 1800s some scholars read Samson as a solar myth; few hold this today.

claude.title: What the mother left out
claude.body: In my reading, the two parts of the angel's message that Samson's mother leaves out when she retells it (Judges 13:7), the razor and the rescue of Israel, are the two things Samson loses. What she adds, "to his dying day," comes true at Gaza. Alter and Exum note the changes; I take them further as a key to the story.

sections.b: Numbers 6 describes a Nazirite vow taken for a time. Samson's is imposed before birth and lasts "to his dying day" (Judges 13:7), and his mother keeps the food rules while pregnant. The story keeps bringing him to vineyards, a drinking feast and dead bodies (Judges 14:5–10; 15:15). The Mishnah later defined a "Samson-Nazirite" who must not cut his hair but may become unclean from the dead (Mishnah Nazir 1:2). When his hair is cut, the LORD leaves him (Judges 16:20).

Israel swore two oaths during the war on Benjamin: to give no daughters to Benjamin, and to kill anyone who did not come (Judges 21:1, 5). Unwilling to break either, the elders destroy Jabesh-gilead and arrange the seizure of the dancers at Shiloh, keeping the words of the oath while breaking its spirit (Judges 21:8–23). With Jephthah's vow (Judges 11:30–40), it shows how Judges views rash oaths.

common: Samson broke his Nazirite vow when he touched the lion's carcass; the Mishnah's view is that a lifelong Samson-type vow did not forbid contact with the dead.

sections.b: The Philistines rule Israel for forty years (Judges 13:1), and Judah's men accept it: "Don't you know the Philistines are our masters?" (Judges 15:11). The Samson stories take place in the border lands of the Shephelah: Timnah (Tel Batash), the Sorek Valley, Lehi, and the coast cities of Ashkelon and Gaza. Israel calls them "the uncircumcised" (Judges 14:3; 15:18). Their rulers bribe Delilah, and they celebrate Samson's capture at a feast for Dagon, an old Semitic god they adopted (Judges 16:23). Excavations at Tell Qasile have found a Philistine temple whose roof rested on two central pillars (Judges 16:26–29).

common: Dagon was a fish god; ancient sources show he was an old Semitic god, likely of grain, worshiped long before the Philistines.

sections.b: The Spirit of the LORD "began to prod" Samson (Judges 13:25) and three times "swept down" on him (Judges 14:6, 19; 15:14), giving strength to kill a lion, thirty men and a thousand Philistines. The same verb is used for Saul and David (1 Samuel 10:6; 16:13). The Spirit's coming gives power for a task without changing Samson's character, and its departure is not noticed by Samson himself (Judges 16:20).
sections.refs: Judges 13:25; Judges 14:6; Judges 14:19; Judges 15:14; Judges 16:20; 1 Samuel 10:6; 1 Samuel 16:13

sections.b: The angel of the LORD appears twice to Manoah's wife, refuses food, will not give his name because it is "wonderful" (Judges 13:18), and rises to heaven in the flame of the offering (Judges 13:20). Manoah concludes, "It is God we have seen!" (Judges 13:22). With Gideon's visitor (Judges 6:11–24), this is one of the fullest angel-of-the-LORD scenes in the Old Testament. Jewish readers usually see a created angel; many Christians since the early church have seen the Son of God.

The book never gives her name, yet she is the one the angel visits twice and the one who reasons rightly that God means them no harm (Judges 13:23). Later tradition named her Eluma (Pseudo-Philo) or Hazzelelponi (Talmud, Bava Batra 91a). Her son, unlike Isaac or Samuel, will disappoint the hopes of his birth story.

After Samson, there are no more judges. Two stories show Israel without any leader: Micah's idol and the Danite migration (Judges 17–18), and the crime at Gibeah and the war on Benjamin (Judges 19–21). They are framed by the refrain "There was no king in Israel in those days" (Judges 17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25), twice with "Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes." Phinehas son of Eleazar is still priest (Judges 20:28) and Moses' grandson serves at Dan (Judges 18:30), so many readers, from Josephus on, place these events early in the period. They come last for their theme.
sections.refs: Judges 17:6; Judges 18:1; Judges 18:30; Judges 19:1; Judges 20:28; Judges 21:25

sections.b: The Samson story opens with the usual words, but Israel never cries out to God (Judges 13:1). Samson is the only judge whose birth is announced, yet he only "begins" the rescue (Judges 13:5), and the Philistines still rule when he dies.

The refrain of Judges' ending has been read three ways: as a plea for monarchy to enforce God's law (Deuteronomy 17:14–20); as a case for David's house against Saul's, since the villains are tied to Gibeah, Benjamin and Jabesh-gilead and the victims to Bethlehem (Brettler, Amit); and as an ironic warning that kings would not cure Israel's heart, since the LORD was meant to be its king (Judges 8:23; Dumbrell). Martin Buber, by contrast, saw Judges as two books joined: an anti-king book built on Gideon's refusal (Judges 8:23) and Jotham's fable, and a pro-king book, chapters 17–21, to which the refrain belongs. The refrain echoes Moses' warning against "each of us doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8).
sections.refs: Judges 17:6; Judges 18:1; Judges 19:1; Judges 21:25; Deuteronomy 12:8; Deuteronomy 17:14–20; Judges 8:23

uncommon: Martin Buber held that Judges joins an anti-king book to a pro-king one, and that the refrain belongs to the pro-king part, chapters 17–21.

sections.h: Micah's idol and the shrine at Dan (Judges 17–18)
sections.b: Micah's mother dedicates stolen silver "to the LORD" to make a carved idol and a cast idol, the very thing the law cursed (Judges 17:3; Deuteronomy 27:15). Micah adds an ephod and household gods and hires a Levite. The Danites steal it all, and Micah cries, "My gods that I made, you've taken them" (Judges 18:24). The idol becomes the shrine of Dan, served by Moses' grandson "until the day the land was taken into exile" (Judges 18:30). This is worship of the LORD in a forbidden form, like Aaron's and Jeroboam's calves.

Micah's shrine holds an ephod and teraphim (Judges 17:5), used for seeking guidance (Judges 18:5). When the Danites carry them off, Micah's cry echoes Laban's "But why did you steal my gods?" (Genesis 31:30; Judges 18:24). Hosea later lists ephod and teraphim among things Israel will lose (Hosea 3:4).

Micah "fills the hand" of his own son as priest, and then of a wandering Levite whom he pays ten pieces of silver a year (Judges 17:5, 10–12). The Danites offer the Levite a whole tribe, and he goes gladly (Judges 18:19–20). He turns out to be Jonathan, grandson of Moses (Judges 18:30). The story shows the priesthood cut loose from the law that tied it to Aaron's family and one sanctuary (Numbers 3:10; Deuteronomy 12:5–14).

With no land it could hold, Dan sent five scouts north. They consulted Micah's Levite, found Laish "calm and trusting" and far from help, and six hundred Danites took Micah's idol and priest, burned Laish and rebuilt it as Dan (Judges 18:1–29). The story follows the pattern of the conquest (spies, report, march, victory) but bends every part. It also explains the origins of the shrine at Dan, later home of Jeroboam's calf.
Samson's family came from Zorah, part of the Danite clan that remained in the south (Judges 13:2). Dan's Camp, Mahaneh-dan, appears both in Samson's story and in the migration (Judges 13:25; 18:12).

The men of Gibeah demand the Levite "so we can know him"; the host offers his daughter and the concubine; the Levite pushes her out, and she is raped all night and dies at the door (Judges 19:22–28). The Levite cuts her body into twelve pieces to summon Israel. The war that follows kills tens of thousands, and Benjamin's survivors are given four hundred women taken from Jabesh-gilead and two hundred dancers seized at Shiloh (Judges 21:10–23). Phyllis Trible's Texts of Terror made this chapter central to feminist reading of the Bible; J. Cheryl Exum and Mieke Bal argue the story itself participates in the violence it shows. Traditional commentators such as Block condemn every man in the story. All agree the text is an indictment of Israel.
sections.refs: Judges 19:22–30; Judges 20:4–6; Judges 21:10–23; Genesis 19:4–8; Genesis 34:1–7; 2 Samuel 13:11–14

sections.b: The verb 'innah, used for the rape of Dinah and Tamar and for what was done to the Levite's concubine (Judges 19:24; 20:5), is used three times of what the Philistines want Delilah to do to Samson: "bring him low" (Judges 16:5, 6, 19). The man who took women as he pleased is humbled by one.

common: The concubine had committed adultery; the Hebrew verb is debated, and the Greek says she became angry (Judges 19:2).
uncommon: Some readers suggest the woman was still alive when the Levite cut her up; the Hebrew does not say she was dead, though the Greek adds it (Judges 19:28).

sections.b: Judges 19:15–25 retells Genesis 19:1–11 almost phrase by phrase: an outsider host, men of the town surrounding the house, the demand to "know" the guest, "my brothers, do not do evil," two women offered, "whatever looks good to you." The differences make the point: no angels rescue anyone, and the woman is thrown out. Israel has become Sodom. Most scholars think Judges 19 was written with Genesis 19 in mind, though Susan Niditch (1982) argued that the Judges version is the more original. Hosea's "days of Gibeah" (Hosea 9:9; 10:9) keep the memory alive.

sections.h: Too much and none at all (Judges 19)
sections.b: In Bethlehem the concubine's father keeps the Levite feasting for five days (Judges 19:4–9). In Gibeah of Benjamin no one takes the travelers in until an old outsider from Ephraim does (Judges 19:15–21). Then the host offers the women of his house to protect his male guest (Judges 19:24). Stuart Lasine called it "Lot's hospitality in an inverted world."

The Danites use the language of conquest against peaceful Laish without offering peace as Deuteronomy 20:10 required (Judges 18:9–10, 27). Israel then uses the ambush of Ai against Gibeah (Judges 20:29–48; Joshua 8), burns it "whole" like a town under the ban (Deuteronomy 13:16), destroys Benjamin's towns, and puts Jabesh-gilead under the ban, sparing only virgins as in the war on Midian (Judges 21:10–12; Numbers 31:17–18). Susan Niditch reads these chapters as a critique of the ban ideology turned on Israel itself.
sections.refs: Judges 18:9–10; Judges 18:27–28; Judges 20:29–48; Judges 21:10–12; Deuteronomy 13:12–18; Deuteronomy 20:10–17; Numbers 31:17–18

sections.h: Shiloh at the end of Judges (Judges 18:31; 21:12–23)
sections.b: Micah's idol stood at Dan "all the time that the house of God stood at Shiloh" (Judges 18:31). The four hundred women of Jabesh are brought to the camp at Shiloh, and the yearly festival of the LORD there becomes the setting for the abduction of its dancing daughters (Judges 21:19–23). The careful directions to Shiloh (Judges 21:19) suggest readers who no longer knew where it was. The Mishnah remembers girls dancing in the vineyards on the 15th of Av (Mishnah Taanit 4:8).

The Levite chose Gibeah over Jebusite Jerusalem because it was Israelite (Judges 19:12). There, no one took him in except an outsider, and the men of the town committed the crime that led to war (Judges 19:15–25). Israel defeated Gibeah with an ambush and burned it "whole" (Judges 20:29–40). The Hebrew sometimes writes Geba where Gibeah seems meant (Judges 20:10, 33).

The concubine's body, cut in twelve pieces, summons the tribes, who gather "like one man" (Judges 19:29; 20:1). The only war in Judges that all Israel fights together is against one of its own tribes. Afterward Israel weeps that "Israel is short one tribe today" (Judges 21:3) and goes to great and terrible lengths to restore Benjamin. The left-handed slingers of Benjamin, "son of the right hand," recall Ehud (Judges 3:15; 20:16).

A pilegesh was a wife of lower rank. The Levite is called her husband and her father his father-in-law (Judges 19:3–4), yet as the story goes on the narrator calls him "her master" (Judges 19:26–27). The Greek and Hebrew disagree on why she left him (Judges 19:2).

"The LORD's festival" held yearly at Shiloh, with dancing in the vineyards, was probably a harvest festival like Booths (Judges 21:19–21; Deuteronomy 16:13–15). The Talmud links the story to the 15th of Av, which it calls the day Benjamin was allowed to marry into the other tribes again (Bavli Taanit 30b).

sections.h: Manoah: "It is God we have seen!" (Judges 13)
sections.b: After the angel rises in the altar flame, Manoah fears death (Judges 13:22). His wife answers that a God who accepted their offering does not mean to kill them (Judges 13:23). The scene follows Gideon's (Judges 6:22–23) and Jacob's (Genesis 32:30).

sections.h: Parallels to the Samson stories and Judges 21
sections.b: Samson's lion and strength recall Heracles and Mesopotamian lion-fighters; his foxes with torches resemble a Roman rite described by Ovid (Fasti 4); the seizure of the dancers at Shiloh resembles Livy's story of the Sabine women (History of Rome 1.9). Most scholars see shared folk motifs rather than borrowing. Dagon was an old Semitic god known from Ebla, Mari and Ugarit.

The rare word for "the knife" (ma'akhelet) appears in Genesis 22:6, 10 and in Judges 19:29, when the Levite cuts up his concubine. Many readers hear a deliberate echo: at Moriah, God stopped the knife; at Gibeah, no one did.

After two defeats by Benjamin, all Israel goes up to Bethel, weeps before the LORD and fasts "until evening," offering burnt offerings and peace offerings before asking again whether to fight (Judges 20:26–28). Here fasting goes with grief, sacrifice and seeking God's word, and the next battle is won.
